job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Grace Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the first year of a master's in power systems at Alder University, and I live with my parents in Pinehaven, about forty minutes by train. My day is a study block in the morning, then simulation work on how a grid copes with lots of solar, and some evenings I help my dad, who runs a small electrical contracting business, with his quotes. I graduated top of my electrical engineering class, with summer placements at the regional grid control room and at a solar installer. I'm applying for graduate schemes in the background. I use an AI tool now and then to summarise papers, and I always check its numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful assistant and nothing more. I'd tell my classmates it saves me an hour on reading papers, but it hasn't changed what the work is. The grid still needs people who understand why a transformer trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm quite relaxed about it. Power systems need a lot of human judgement and licensing, and the sector is hiring because of the energy transition. My worry is more ordinary: graduate schemes get hundreds of applicants and I have a loan of around 11,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, finish the thesis on solar and storage, and send eight or nine scheme applications by February. I'd carry on helping my dad with quotes on Saturdays and keep using the summarising tool for reading. If the schemes fall through, I'd try the solar installer I interned at, Brightfield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little nervous about the applications but nothing I can't handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound secure. What would make you less so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the schemes all said no. I'd still be fine because of my parents, but it would sting, and I'd start to wonder if top marks mean much. I haven't had a rejection yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who helps you most with the job search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad has contacts in the trade, but he's not much help with graduate schemes. My old placement supervisor, Mr Okoro, has read my cover letters twice, and he's been the most useful.

say: AI is a **handy assistant**, but it hasn't changed what grid work is.
The sector is hiring because of the **energy transition**.
think: Power systems need **human judgement** and licences, so I feel fairly safe.
My real worry is crowded **graduate schemes** and an 11,000 loan.
do: Apply to eight or nine **graduate schemes** by February.
Keep helping my dad with **quotes** on Saturdays.
Use the summarising tool for **reading** only.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with some nerves about the applications.
S0.quote: The grid still needs people who understand why a transformer trips.
fieldNote: Grace's calm comes from a **sector** that is hiring and a family safety net around her.
Her only stated worry is ordinary competition for **graduate schemes**, which she would face with or without AI.

steps.text: Send eight or nine graduate scheme applications by February
Keep doing Saturday quotes for dad's contracting business
Finish the solar and storage thesis on schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and that we should be honest about it. Writing, checking and planning tasks are exactly what junior engineers do in their first two years, so some of that moves to software. I'd also say the energy sector will probably adapt more slowly than a bank would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it changes my first job more than my career. Fewer juniors might be hired to do the drawings and the load calculations, and the ones who are hired will be expected to supervise the tool. That's good for me if I get in and bad if I'm the one left outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a course in grid data and machine learning this year, so I can supervise the tools rather than be replaced by them. I'd apply more widely, including to the solar installer and my local distribution company. And I'd ask my professor, Dr Lindqvist, whether a PhD place would be a smart way to wait out a thin year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'll be fine, but it's the year I have the least control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is it about the first two years of a job that software can take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The calculation sheets, the drawing checks and the first draft of a report are tedious, which is exactly why a firm would hand them over. I did all of those at my placement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a PhD. Is that a plan or a hiding place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both, and I know it. I'd only do it if the topic is something I care about, like grid storage. If it's just to avoid the job market, I'd stop myself.

say: Junior engineering tasks like **checking** and calculations will move to software.
Energy will probably adapt **more slowly** than a bank.
think: This changes my **first job** more than my career.
Juniors who can **supervise** the tools will have the edge.
do: Take a grid data and **machine learning** course.
Apply more widely, including **solar** installers and the local distribution company.
Ask Dr Lindqvist about a **PhD** as a fallback.
feel: **Uneasy**, because it's the year I have the least control.
S1.quote: The calculation sheets, the drawing checks and the first draft of a report are tedious, which is exactly why a firm would hand them over.
fieldNote: Grace thinks in terms of what a **junior** actually does all day, which makes her answers concrete.
She is honest that a **PhD** could be both a plan and a hiding place.

steps.text: Take an online course on machine learning for grid data
Apply to the solar installer and the local distribution company
Ask Dr Lindqvist whether a PhD fits a thin hiring year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and put rules in place for the critical stuff, like the grid, hospitals and water. If thinking work is automated in two years, then someone has to decide who is responsible when it goes wrong. I'd say that publicly, even though it won't make me popular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately my stomach drops. The entry-level job I'm aiming for, running studies on a network model, is just the sort of thing a system does faster. I'd be 26 when robots can do the physical side, so I'm not safe long term either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my savings, about 2,500, into a safe account and stop spending on anything extra. I'd apply straight away to the grid control room where I interned, because licensed operators and safety-critical roles will be among the last to hand over. And I'd ask my dad whether I could join his firm properly, since wiring a building still needs a human for a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like running for a train that's already moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd join your dad's firm. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not what I planned, but it's honest work and the business could use someone who understands solar and batteries. My dad would be thrilled and say nothing, which is how he is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd tell your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum that I'm okay and that I have a plan. Then I'd probably cry in the bathroom, because I'd also be unsure.

say: Critical systems like the **grid** need rules and clear responsibility.
Two years is too fast for **governments** and families.
think: The **entry-level** network studies I'm aiming for are what a system does faster.
Even with robots later, I'm not **safe** long term.
do: Move my **2,500** savings into a safe account.
Apply at once to the **grid control room** where I interned.
Ask my dad about joining his **firm** properly.
feel: **Anxious**, like running for a train already moving.
S2.quote: I'd be 26 when robots can do the physical side, so I'm not safe long term either.
fieldNote: Grace's plan runs through **safety-critical** roles and the family firm, both places where humans stay longer.
Her public calm gives way to private **fear** about the entry-level job.

steps.text: Move the 2,500 in savings into a safe account
Apply to the grid control room where I interned
Ask dad to take me on in his contracting firm
Write to my local representative about rules for critical systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare if people actually do it. Governments should pay for retraining and make sure the grid and other infrastructure stay under human control. I'd also encourage friends not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy but not scared. By 2031 I'd be 29 with a few years of work behind me and maybe a professional engineering registration in progress. That feels like standing on firm ground when the change arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a scheme job, even if it's not my dream one, and work towards chartered status. I'd learn to build and check AI tools used in grid planning, so I'm the person who knows how it works. I'd keep saving about 300 a month, and maybe buy a small flat share in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. I can picture myself being useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does chartered status protect you from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chartered status makes me someone who signs things off, and that carries legal responsibility. A firm can't easily hand that to a machine, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if it were two years instead of five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the long route. I'd go straight to my dad's firm or a control-room role and hold on. Five years lets me do things in a nicer order.

say: Five years is enough to **prepare** if governments actually fund retraining.
Critical infrastructure should stay under **human control**, and I'd tell friends not to panic.
think: By 2031 I'd have **years of work** behind me, which feels like firm ground.
do: Take a scheme job and work towards **chartered** status.
Learn how AI tools in grid **planning** are built and checked.
feel: **Uneasy** but steady, able to picture being useful.
S3.quote: Chartered status makes me someone who signs things off, and that carries legal responsibility.
fieldNote: Grace's plan leans on **professional registration**, which she sees as a legal shield against automation.
With five years, her path is more orderly and less **desperate** than in the two-year case.

steps.text: Take a graduate scheme job and start the chartered engineer route
Learn how AI planning tools for the grid are built and checked
Save 300 a month towards a share in a small flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, so let's use it on purpose. I'd push for a proper plan on retraining, and I'd say people should use these tools instead of fearing them. I'd also joke that I'll be the one fixing the robots' charging stations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be calm. By 2036 I'd be 34, hopefully settled, hopefully with a family, and well into my career. I'd still keep a bit of fear in my pocket about the 3 years after, when robots reach hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work for several years, and pay off the loan quickly. I'd build experience in storage and flexible demand, which will matter whatever happens. I'd keep a side skill with wiring and installation, because I can always do that with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. It feels like the normal worries of a career, and not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the long timeline that you don't trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that people will actually use it well. Ten years can disappear if no one plans. So I'd stay involved in my union branch to push for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you want children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, one day. I'd like to be established first, so the long timeline is a relief. With two years I'd be putting off thoughts like that.

say: We have **time**, so we should plan retraining on purpose.
People should **use** the tools instead of fearing them.
think: By 2036 I could be **settled** and well into my career.
I keep a bit of fear about **robots** reaching hands-on work later.
do: Finish the master's and pay off the **loan** quickly.
Build experience in **storage** and flexible demand.
Keep my **wiring** skills as a fallback.
feel: **Mostly calm**, like the normal worries of a career.
S4.quote: Ten years can disappear if no one plans.
fieldNote: Grace stays **calm** because she can picture a settled adult life, with a family, inside the timeline.
She worries about **follow-through** by governments and employers, not the technology itself.

steps.text: Pay off the 11,000 loan within five years of starting work
Specialise in grid storage and flexible demand
Join the union branch and press for funded retraining
Settle in a steady job before planning a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's no time to get a first job and a track record. What would help is guaranteed retraining, rules that keep humans in charge of critical systems, and a clear route for graduates into safety-critical work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I keep thinking my parents' support is my luck, not my merit. I'd like to be useful to people who don't have that.

headlineQuote: I keep thinking my parents' support is my luck, not my merit.
portrait: Grace is a 24-year-old **electrical engineering** graduate doing a master's in power systems, living with her parents.
She uses AI tools sometimes, checks their numbers, and sees the **grid** as a slow-changing, human-supervised sector.
Her dad's contracting firm and her placements give her **fallbacks** most graduates lack.
Her mood runs from calm to **anxious** at two years, and back to calm at ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time for a first job or track record.
whatWouldHelp: Guaranteed **retraining**, human control of critical systems and a route into safety-critical work.
